links.note: 391 asks for two things in order: learn without flaw (கசடறக் கற்க), then stand in keeping with it (நிற்க அதற்குத் தக). 834 names the person who does the first and skips the second: one who has studied, understood and even taught others but is not himself restrained (தானடங்கா) is the greatest of fools. The pair shows that the second half of 391 is not an afterthought: learning without it is classed as folly.

391 says to stand in keeping with what one has learned. 140 says those who have not learned to live in accord with the world (உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் கல்லார்) are without understanding even though they have studied much (பலகற்றும்). Both measure learning by the conduct that follows it, and 140 turns the verb 'learn' itself toward conduct.

391 treats right conduct as what should follow flawless learning. 823, on false friends, says that even after studying many good things (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்தும்) it is hard for the unworthy (மாணார்) to become good at heart. It limits 391: study does not by itself produce the standing-by-it, which is why 391 has to command it separately.

392 calls numbers and letters, 'these two' (இவ்விரண்டும்), the eyes of living beings. 581 calls spies and the respected treatise, 'these two' (இவையிரண்டும்), the king's eyes (மன்னவன் கண்). The same two-eyes figure is used for every person and then for the ruler, and in both one eye is book knowledge; the king's second eye is live report.

392 makes numbers and letters the eyes of the living. 445 says a king goes about with his counsellors as his eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக) and so must choose them with care. Both treat sight as something acquired from outside oneself, through learning in one case and through chosen advisers in the other.

393 says only the learned have eyes; the unlearned have two sores on the face (முகத்திரண்டு புண்ணுடையர்). 575 says kindly regard is the eye's ornament and without it the eye is recognised as a sore (புண்ணென்று உணரப்படும்). The same eye-or-sore figure is applied to two different things, learning and kindly regard, so the book gives two separate tests for whether an eye is an eye.

393 denies real eyes to the unlearned. 418 says ears not pierced by listening (கேள்வியால் தோட்கப்படாத செவி) are of a deaf kind even though they hear. The next chapter repeats the pattern for the other sense: an organ counts only when it has been trained by learning or listening.

394 says the work of the learned is to meet so that others are glad and to part so that others think of them (உள்ளப் பிரிதல்). 839 says, ironically, that friendship with fools is very sweet because parting from them (பிரிவின்கண்) brings no pain at all. Both judge a person by what the parting leaves behind; the fool is the case where it leaves nothing.

394 describes the learned as people whose company others want again after it ends. 643 defines speech as what binds those who heard it and makes even those who did not hear want it (கேளாரும் வேட்ப). 643 gives the means, speech, for the effect 394 describes.

395 uses the poor standing before the rich (உடையார்முன் இல்லார்போல்) as its figure for the learner, and on Parimelazhagar's reading those who learned standing so are foremost while those who would not are lowest. 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking (இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்), even asking water for a cow. Read together, the posture the book calls degrading when the object is goods is the one it honours when the object is learning.

395 praises learning in the stance of one who lacks before one who has. 724 tells even the learned to state what they have learned before the learned and take more from those who know more (மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்). The asking stance of 395 is thus not only for beginners; it continues among the learned.

396 says understanding wells up in proportion to what one has learned (கற்றனைத்து ஊறும் அறிவு), as a sand-well gives water as far as it is dug. 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own real understanding still prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்). If உண்மையறிவு is read with Parimelazhagar and Pope as the understanding fate has allotted, 373 caps what study can add, against 396's open-ended proportion.

396 says understanding grows with each bit of learning. 1110, a lover's speech, uses as its comparison that with each thing known one sees one's earlier not-knowing (அறிதோறு அறியாமை கண்டற்று). The comparison carries a view of learning that adds to 396: what increases with learning includes the awareness of how much was not known.

396 uses spring water in a dug sand-well (மணற்கேணி ... ஊறும்) for understanding that rises the more one learns. 1161 has a woman say that the pain she would hide rises like spring water for those who bale it out (இறைப்பவர்க்கு ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்). The same image of a spring that gives more the more it is drawn serves for knowledge in one place and for love's pain in the other.

397 says that for the learned any land is one's land and any town one's town (யாதானும் நாடாம் ஊராம்). 753 says the unfailing lamp called wealth goes to whatever country one has in mind (எண்ணிய தேயத்துச் சென்று) and cuts away the darkness there. Learning and wealth are each credited with making foreign places open to a person.

398 says learning acquired in one birth is a protection in seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). 126 ends with the same words: drawing in the five senses like a tortoise in one birth is a protection in seven. The shared formula puts learning beside sense-restraint as the two things said to carry over as a safeguard.

398 says what is learned in one span protects through seven. 835 says a fool can, in one span's doing (ஒருமைச் செயல்), make the mire he will sink in for seven (எழுமையும்). The same one-to-seven reckoning is run in the opposite direction, with folly in the place of learning.

398 has learning protect a person across seven births. 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing (கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார்) reach the path of not coming back here. 356 takes learning one step past 398: joined to seeing the real, it ends the births that 398 says it guards.

399 says the learned, seeing the world take delight in what delights themselves, love it more; Parimelazhagar takes 'it' to be learning. 68 says one's children's understanding is sweeter to all living beings than to oneself (தம்மின் ... மன்னுயிர்க்கெல்லாம் இனிது). Both treat knowledge as a good whose pleasure is shared by the world and not kept by its holder.

399 assumes the learned person's learning gives the world joy. 650 says those who cannot unfold what they have learned so that others grasp it (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like a cluster of flowers in bloom without scent. It adds the condition 399 leaves unstated: the world's delight depends on being able to convey the learning.

400 says learning is the imperishable, excellent wealth and other things are not wealth (மாடல்ல மற்றையவை). 411 says the wealth of the ear is the wealth among wealths and the head of them all (செல்வத்துளெல்லாம் தலை). Adjacent chapters use the same 'true wealth' figure for study and then for listening, without ranking the two against each other.

400 calls learning wealth that cannot be destroyed (கேடில்) and denies the name to the rest. 592 says possession of inner drive is possession, while possession of goods does not stay and slips away (நில்லாது நீங்கிவிடும்). Both set an inner possession against goods on the ground of permanence.

400 gives the title of real wealth to learning. 241 gives it to grace (அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம்), with the reason that wealth of goods is found even among the base. The same move appears in the Book of Virtue with a different winner, and 241's reason, who can hold it, differs from 400's, whether it can be lost.

401 says holding forth in an assembly without full book-learning (நிரம்பிய நூலின்றிக் கோட்டி கொளல்) is like playing dice without a marked board. 728 says those who have learned many things are still of no use if they cannot speak well and tellingly in a good assembly. Together they give both halves: speech without learning has nothing to stand on, and learning without speech yields nothing.

402 compares the unlearned man's desire to speak (சொற்காமுறுதல், as Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read it) to a woman without breasts desiring womanhood. 727 compares the learning of one who fears the assembly to a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி among enemies. Both use a figure of lacking what one's role requires, and they cover the two opposite failures: wanting to speak without learning, and having learning without the nerve to speak. Kalaignar reads 402 differently, as desiring to hear the unlearned man's words.

403 says even the unlearned are very good if they can keep from speaking before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 715 says the best of all good things is the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு). 715 turns the rule 403 gives the unlearned into a general virtue of the assembly that binds capable speakers too.

403 counts silence before the learned as the unlearned person's merit. 729 says those who have studied and understood yet fear an assembly of the good are lower than the unlearned (கல்லாதவரின் கடை). Silence is therefore not good in itself: it is right for the one with nothing to say and a failing in the one who has something.

404 says that however good an unlearned person's brightness (ஒட்பம்) may be, those with understanding do not accept it. 423 says understanding is seeing the true substance of a thing from whoever's mouth it is heard (யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும்). If 404 means the wise set aside what the unlearned say even when it is good, it conflicts with 423's rule to judge the matter and not the speaker; on Parimelazhagar's reading, that they only decline to credit him with real brightness because an occasional hit is accidental, the conflict is smaller.

404 says native brightness without learning is not accepted by the wise. 636 says nothing over-subtle can stand before those who have keen native intelligence together with book-learning (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்). 636 states positively what 404 implies: natural intelligence gains its force when joined to study.

405 says the unlearned person's self-regard gives way when he engages and speaks (சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்); Parimelazhagar supplies that the talk is with a learned person. 1046 says that even when the poor speak of good matters well understood, their words go slack (சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்). The same closing phrase marks two ways speech fails: in 405 for want of learning in the speaker, in 1046 for want of standing with the hearers, though the content is sound.

405 says an unlearned person's standing collapses once he converses. 717 says the learning of those who have studied and understood shines out (விளங்கும்) among those able to examine words without fault. Conversation with the competent is the test in both, with opposite results for the unlearned and the learned.

406 says the unlearned are no more than 'they exist' (உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர்) and are like barren saline ground that yields nothing. 730 says those who, fearing the arena, cannot convey what they have learned are, though they exist, equal to those who do not (உளரெனினும் இல்லாரொடு ஒப்பர்). The same bare-existence wording puts the learned who cannot speak in nearly the place of the unlearned.

406 grants the unlearned existence only and compares them to land that yields nothing (பயவாக் களர்). 572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a burden to the earth (உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை). Both reduce a person lacking a quality to mere existence and express it through land, as barren soil in one and as weight on the ground in the other.

407 compares the good looks of one without fine, penetrating understanding to a well-decorated clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). 1020 compares the movements of those with no shame within to a wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை) made to seem alive by its string. Both use a doll for a human form missing its inner part, understanding in one and shame in the other.

407 says fine appearance without understanding is a doll's beauty. 79 asks what all the outer parts can do for those who lack love, the inner part of the body (அகத்துறுப்பு அன்பிலவர்க்கு). The Book of Virtue makes love the inner thing that gives the body its point; the Book of Wealth makes it trained understanding.

407 says good looks without understanding are worth what a clay doll's are. 667 says not to scorn anyone on seeing their form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை), since the great chariot has its small linchpin. Both deny that appearance measures a person, 407 for the handsome and empty, 667 for the slight and capable.

408 says wealth lodged with the unlearned (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு) is more painful than poverty lodged with the good. 837 shows what happens when a fool gets great wealth: strangers feast and his own people go hungry. 837 gives one concrete form of the harm; Manakkudavar likewise reads 408 as harm done to others.

408 says wealth is worse than poverty when it sits with the unlearned (வறுமையின் இன்னாதே). 558 says having is more painful than not having (இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை) under a ruler who does no justice. Both invert the usual ranking of wealth over poverty under a stated condition: the holder's lack of learning in one, the king's injustice in the other.

408 complains of wealth with the unlearned and poverty with the good. 374 says the world has two separate natures: wealth is one thing and being clear-minded another (திருவேறு தெள்ளியராதலும் வேறு). The fate chapter states as the way of the world the mismatch that 408 calls painful.

409 says the unlearned, though born high, do not have the worth (பாடு) of the learned born low. 133 says having conduct is good family, and lapse from it becomes low birth (இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்). Both make birth give way to something acquired, learning in 409 and conduct in 133.

409 ranks the low-born learned above the high-born unlearned. 973 says those who are not high are not high even when placed above, and those who are not low are not low even when placed below (மேலிருந்தும் மேலல்லார் மேலல்லர்). 973 states generally what 409 states for learning: position does not settle rank.

410 says others stand to those who have studied the shining books as beasts stand to people (விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர்). 420 calls those who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear மாக்கள், and asks what it matters whether they die or live. The next chapter carries the comparison on, from those who have not studied to those who do not even listen.

410 makes book-learning the difference between people and beasts. 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for any living being, and that the distinction of human beings is having shame (நாணுடைமை மாந்தர் சிறப்பு). The two verses give different answers, learning and shame, to what sets humans apart.

410 says the unlearned differ from the learned as beasts from people, though all are human in form. 1071 says the base look exactly like people (மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர்), a likeness the speaker has seen nowhere else. Both deny full human standing to some who have the human shape, for lack of learning in one and for baseness in the other.
